title: The Abbreviator's Circuit: Exile, the Travelling Curia, and the Building Written Down as Number
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Genoa, born under the Florentine ban
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Grayson and Argan) for Genoa and 1404. Some English sources give 18 February rather than 14 February; the disagreement is recorded and not resolved here. No parish, street, or house of birth is documented: the pin is Genoa Cathedral (San Lorenzo), 44.4075/8.9316, used as the city's central landmark and not as a birth site. The research pool's 44.4085/8.931 was about 120 metres north of the cathedral and is corrected here.
stops.campa: The Alberti are bankers and the Alberti are banned. Florence exiled the family and the ban still holds, so Lorenzo di Benedetto conducts his business from Genoa, and here his second son is born to Bianca Fieschi, outside marriage. They call the boy Battista. He will not stand in the city his surname belongs to until he is thirty. Two disabilities in law attach to him at birth, exile and illegitimacy. No register names the street, the parish or the house he is born in.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti' (Grayson and Argan)
English Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The Alberti family's exile from Florence and its mercantile houses at Genoa and Venice

stops.name: Venice, the exiles' counting house
stops.date_confidence: The move to Venice is attested (DBI); the exact residence is not documented and the pin is the city. Some accounts tie the move to plague at Genoa, and the pool treats that causal link as less secure than the move itself. Year approximate, month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The household moves to Venice, where Lorenzo keeps the trade running under the same ban. Battista's childhood passes among ledgers, correspondents and bills of exchange, the machinery of a merchant house that operates everywhere except at home. He learns his Latin and he learns the arithmetic of a counting room, and afterwards the two never come apart in him. Some accounts tie the move north to plague at Genoa; the move itself is better attested than any reason given for it. Which quarter of Venice held the family, and for exactly how long, nobody wrote down.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Lorenzo di Benedetto Alberti's Venetian business during the family's exile

stops.name: Padua, the school of Gasparino Barzizza
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that Alberti studied under Barzizza at Padua with Barbaro, Filelfo and Beccadelli among his fellows; the years are given as roughly 1416 to 1418 and the month and day are defaulted to 01. Barzizza kept a private boarding school, not a university faculty, and its schoolroom is not located; the pin is Palazzo Bo, 45.4072/11.8778, purely as a city stand-in. Palazzo Bo only became the university's seat in 1493, after Alberti's death, so the pin is a landmark and not a place he entered. The pool's 45.4064/11.8768 is corrected.
stops.campa: He is sent inland to Padua, to the boarding school of Gasparino Barzizza, where Latin is taught as Cicero wrote it rather than as the notaries use it. His fellow pupils include Francesco Barbaro, Francesco Filelfo, and Antonio Beccadelli of Palermo, who will later do him a peculiar service. The formation is literary and rhetorical from end to end. Nothing in it touches a mason's yard or a painter's bottega. Where he learned what he later wrote about painting and about building, the record does not say.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Gasparino Barzizza's Paduan boarding school and its alumni

stops.name: Padua, the death of Lorenzo Alberti
stops.date_confidence: Date and place attested (DBI). The murder attempt by relatives rests solely on the anonymous fifteenth-century Vita and on a document Girolamo Mancini read as circumstantial support; no named perpetrator, judicial finding or prosecution is documented, and the pool retains it only as a flagged tradition. Pin as above, the city and not the house.
stops.campa: Lorenzo di Benedetto Alberti dies at Padua on the twenty-eighth of May. His sons are left to relatives who contest the inheritance, and the money that paid for Padua and is meant to pay for Bologna becomes a thing to be litigated over. The anonymous life written in the next generation says the relatives went past lawsuits and tried to have the young man killed. No court record, no name and no finding survives to carry that. What is documented is the lawsuit and the shortage of money it caused him.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
anonymous fifteenth-century Vita of Alberti, as reported and qualified in the DBI entry
suggested_refs: The Alberti inheritance dispute of the 1420s and Girolamo Mancini's archival biography

segments.name: Bologna: Canon Law and a Forged Comedy

stops.name: Bologna, the law that spends his memory
stops.date_confidence: Study of canon law at Bologna from about 1421 is attested (DBI, English Wikipedia). The illness and its causes come from the anonymous Vita, a self-fashioning source and not a medical record; no modern diagnosis is possible from the evidence. Month and day are ordering defaults. Pin corrected to Piazza Galvani and the Archiginnasio, 44.4922/11.3436; the pool's 44.4939/11.3427 falls on Piazza Maggiore. The Archiginnasio itself was only built in 1562, so 'seat of the medieval Studium' is anachronistic and the pin is a city stand-in: in Alberti's day the law schools were dispersed across Bologna.
stops.campa: He reads canon law at the Studium, the discipline that will license him to hold benefices and pay him for the rest of his life. He hates it. The anonymous life describes years of sickness through this stretch and blames overwork, the strain of holding statutes in the head, and the hostility of his family, and it has him turning to mathematics because number asked less of a memory the law had emptied. That is a self-portrait dressed as a biography. Whether he was actually ill, and of what, no physician set down.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
anonymous fifteenth-century Vita of Alberti, as summarized in the DBI entry
suggested_refs: The anonymous Vita of Alberti, probable self-authorship and its account of the Bologna years

stops.name: Bologna, Philodoxeos under another man's name
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that Alberti drafted the Philodoxeos fabula at Bologna in the 1420s and that Beccadelli circulated it as an ancient work by 'Lepidus', Alberti acknowledging it roughly a decade later. The year is approximate; month and day defaulted to 01. Pin as above.
stops.campa: He writes a Latin comedy, Philodoxeos fabula, the lover of glory. Beccadelli, his schoolfellow from Barzizza's schoolroom at Padua, gets hold of a defective copy and puts it into circulation as an ancient text by an author called Lepidus. Humanist Italy reads it as a Roman play and admires it as one. Alberti lets the attribution stand about ten years before claiming the comedy as his own. The version that carried its reputation through that decade was the faulty copy.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Philodoxeos fabula and its circulation as the work of 'Lepidus'

stops.name: Bologna, doctor of canon law
stops.date_confidence: The 1428 doctorate is attested (DBI, English Wikipedia); month and day defaulted to 01. The subsequent French and German embassy under Cardinals Aleman and Albergati, with a return by way of Basel, is an older biographical tradition explicitly rejected by the DBI entry: Alberti appears in no documented suite at the Peace of Arras or at the Council of Basel. It is therefore recorded here in the confidence field and given no stop of its own.
stops.campa: He takes the doctorate in canon law. It is the credential that will carry him into the papal chancery, secure him ecclesiastical income, and leave him free to spend fifty years writing about painting, building, horses, flies, statues, ciphers and the running of households. Older biographies send him next through France and Germany in a cardinal's suite and home by way of Basel. Modern scholarship finds him in no documented retinue at Arras or at Basel and rejects the journey. Where he was between 1428 and 1431 is not known.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The DBI's rejection of the Aleman and Albergati embassy tradition

segments.name: The Curia and the Measured City

stops.name: Rome, secretary to the patriarch of Grado
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that Alberti served Biagio Molin, patriarch of Grado and regent of the papal chancery, who secured his appointment as apostolic abbreviator; the arrival is given as 1432 and possibly already 1431, and the month and day are defaulted to 01. The pin is the Vatican and papal curia precinct; the curia's premises shifted and no single building is documented for him.
stops.campa: He enters the papal curia as secretary to Biagio Molin, patriarch of Grado and regent of the chancery, and through him is made an apostolic abbreviator, one of the men who draft and dress papal documents in the correct Latin formulas. The office pays, and the office is Latin, and Latin is what he has. Rome around him is a town of perhaps thirty thousand people camped in the ruins of a city built for a million. The chancery will employ him for the next thirty-two years.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The office of apostolic abbreviator and the papal chancery under Eugenius IV

stops.name: Rome, the impediment lifted
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI, English Wikipedia): before October 1432 Eugenius IV issued a dispensation removing the canonical disability of Alberti's illegitimate birth, permitting orders and benefices. The exact date within that window is not documented; September is an ordering default within the attested 'before October' bound.
stops.campa: Before October the pope signs away the impediment. Eugenius IV grants a dispensation cancelling the canonical disability of illegitimate birth, so that Battista may take orders and hold benefices. The circumstance of his birth, which no act of his produced and no effort of his could alter, is undone by a document. He is now eligible for orders and for the income of a benefice. The dispensation is issued at some point before October; the day inside that window nobody recorded.
stops.quote: He lived honourably and like a gentleman, as he was, all the course of his life.
stops.quote_source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, life of Leon Batista Alberti (Wikisource translation), written some eighty years after Alberti's death
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The papal dispensation of 1432 removing the disability of illegitimate birth

stops.name: Rome, the life of Saint Potitus
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI): the Vita Sancti Potiti was written for Molin as the first of a planned series of saints' lives that Alberti apparently abandoned, and a letter to Leonardo Dati voices his historical doubts about the legendary material. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Molin sets him to write the life of Saint Potitus, a martyr whose acts survive only as legend, meant as the first in a chancery series of saints' lives. He finishes it, and it is the only one he ever writes. In a letter to his friend Leonardo Dati he says what he thinks of the material: the legends will not stand as history, and he does not know how to write them as though they would. Whether Molin asked him for a second life, and whether he refused it, is not documented either way.
stops.quote: Even sensible people, when they attempt to penetrate the secrets of the Divinity, become as little children.
stops.quote_source: Alberti, Favole, 'Il Fanciullo, i Raggi del Sole, e l'Ombra'; Italian: 'Anche le persone ben sensate, quando voglion penetrare i secreti Divini, si fanno simili a i bambini.' English rendering as carried on Wikiquote, translator uncredited
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Alberti's letter to Leonardo Dati on the historical value of the Potitus legend

stops.name: Rome, the city taken down in angles and radii
stops.date_confidence: The Descriptio urbis Romae is attested (DBI) and its polar or radial coordinate method is the general consensus of architectural history; the survey is dated only loosely to the early or middle 1430s and the month and day are ordering defaults. The Forum pin marks the ruins he worked among rather than a documented station point: the treatise's own centre is generally taken to be the Capitoline.
stops.campa: He walks the ruins with a surveying instrument of his own devising and takes bearings on the standing monuments from a single fixed centre. The result, the Descriptio urbis Romae, is not a drawing. It is a table of angles and distances from which any reader anywhere can lay the plan of Rome out again on his own floor, at any size, with no copyist's hand between him and the city. Nothing in it can be spoiled by a bad draughtsman. While he takes his bearings, the marble of the monuments he is recording is going into the lime kilns.
stops.quote: Leon Batista was well versed in arithmetic, and a very good geometrician.
stops.quote_source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, life of Leon Batista Alberti (Wikisource translation)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Descriptio urbis Romae and its polar coordinate table of the city

stops.name: Rome, the pope rowed down the Tiber
stops.date_confidence: Corrects the research pool, which dated the flight to June 1434 but placed it at Florence. Eugenius IV fled Rome on 4 June 1434, reached Pisa on 12 June, and only reached Florence in October 1434 (English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'). The June stop is therefore Rome, the flight itself; the Florentine arrival is a separate stop dated October. That Alberti travelled with the papal court is attested (DBI).
stops.campa: Rome rises against Eugenius IV, with the Colonna and the Fortebracci pressing him, and on the fourth of June the pope is got out of the city in disguise and rowed down the Tiber under a shield of arrows to a ship waiting at Ostia. The curia follows overland as best it can. Alberti, whose salary and office and dispensation all issue from this one man, goes with the court. He has been in Rome barely three years and has just finished measuring it. He will be out of it for nine.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'
suggested_refs: The flight of Eugenius IV from Rome, 4 June 1434, and the exile of the curia

segments.name: Florence, the City of the Ban

stops.name: Florence, arriving with the exiled court
stops.date_confidence: Eugenius IV reached Florence in October 1434 (English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'), correcting the pool's June dating for the Florentine arrival. That Alberti there renewed or formed relations with Brunelleschi, Donatello, Ghiberti and Luca della Robbia, and met an artistic world altered by Masaccio, is attested (DBI). Day defaulted to 01. Pin is the Piazza San Giovanni and Duomo precinct.
stops.campa: The court reaches Florence in October, and the man whose family was banished from it before he was born walks in beside the pope, thirty years old and seeing the city for the first time. The ban has lapsed. He finds Brunelleschi's dome closed over the cathedral, Donatello and Ghiberti at work, Luca della Robbia glazing terracotta, and walls left by Masaccio that make everything painted before them look flat. Masaccio has been dead six years and was twenty-six when he died.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'
suggested_refs: The Florentine artistic circle of the 1430s: Brunelleschi, Donatello, Ghiberti, Luca della Robbia, Masaccio

stops.name: Florence, the books on the family
stops.date_confidence: The research pool contradicts itself and the contradiction is left standing: its chronology lens places the drafting of the first three books of Della famiglia at Rome in 1433-34, its geography lens at Florence in 1434-36. Both derive from the DBI. The ninety-day claim is the anonymous Vita's, tagged R by the pool and not independently verified; Book IV is dated to about 1440-41. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: He writes the books on the family, a dialogue in Tuscan among Alberti men on money, marriage, the raising of children, and how a house holds together across generations. The family he stages discussing thrift and mutual duty is the family that exiled his father, litigated against his inheritance and left him poor. He gives them a doctrine they did not practise and sets it in their own mouths and their own tongue. The anonymous life says the first three books took ninety days in his thirtieth year.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
anonymous fifteenth-century Vita of Alberti, as reported in the DBI entry
suggested_refs: I libri della famiglia, books I-III, and the disputed ninety-day tradition

stops.name: Florence, the treatise on painting
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI, English Wikipedia) for 1435 and for the Latin dedication to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga and the Tuscan prologue praising Brunelleschi, Donatello, Ghiberti and Luca della Robbia. The priority of the Latin over the Tuscan version is disputed in the scholarship (Bertolini) and is not adjudicated here. Month and day are ordering defaults. The English of the quote is Harbottle and Dalbiac's 1904 rendering; their attribution to Della Pittura III could not be verified against any published edition or translation of the work, since the archive.org copies of Grayson and Spencer are lending-restricted and expose no full-text search.
stops.campa: He writes a treatise on painting in Latin and then again in Tuscan, laying down the visual pyramid, the intersecting plane, and the construction that puts a floor of receding tiles under a painted scene by rule instead of by eye. The Latin goes to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga. The Tuscan opens by praising Brunelleschi, Donatello, Ghiberti and Luca della Robbia, addressed to men who can read it. A writer who has never held a brush hands the painters of Florence the geometry of what they are already doing.
stops.quote: We should respect the gifts that nature gives us, and seek to add to them by industry, study and practice.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Alberti, Della Pittura III, in Harbottle and Dalbiac, Dictionary of Quotations (French and Italian), 1904, p. 352; the attribution is the dictionary's and is unverified against the work
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
Harbottle and Dalbiac, Dictionary of Quotations (French and Italian), 1904
suggested_refs: De pictura and Della pittura, and the disputed priority of the Latin and Tuscan versions

segments.name: The Court That Would Not Sit Still

stops.name: Bologna, after the pope a second time
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) for April 1436; day defaulted to 01. Pin as for the earlier Bologna stops, a city stand-in and not a documented address.
stops.campa: The court moves again, to Bologna, and Alberti moves with it. He has been a papal official for four years and has yet to spend two consecutive years in one city. The chancery travels with the pope: the seals, the registers, the abbreviators and their formulas, an office that exists wherever Eugenius happens to be standing. He is back in the town where he took his degree, on nobody's business but the pope's. The manuscripts he is working on travel in the baggage.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The itinerant chancery of Eugenius IV, 1434-1443

stops.name: Ferrara, the council and Leonello d'Este
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) for January 1438; day defaulted to 01. Pin corrected to the Castello Estense, 44.8375/11.6194 (English Wikipedia, 'Castello Estense'); the pool's 44.8358/11.6199 sits about 190 metres south, essentially on the cathedral, and appears to have been interpolated between the two landmarks. The pin marks the Este court rather than the council's session hall.
stops.campa: The council for the reunion of the Latin and Greek churches opens at Ferrara, and the curia comes north to it, Greeks and Latins disputing the procession of the Holy Spirit in a town belonging to the Este. Alberti attends on the chancery and renews his acquaintance with Leonello d'Este, who reads Latin, keeps scholars, and will shortly ask him about a monument to his father. That conversation is the beginning of the princely commissions. His own work at Ferrara is drafting documents for the council.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Castello Estense'
suggested_refs: The Council of Ferrara, 1438, and the court of Leonello d'Este

stops.name: Florence, Santa Maria Novella and the council removed
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that plague forced the transfer of the council from Ferrara to Florence in 1439 and that Alberti followed the papal court. Month and day are defaults. Santa Maria Novella is used as the landmark because the sessions of the Council of Florence are traditionally sited there; the pin, 43.7746/11.2493, is the same one carried by the later facade stop.
stops.campa: Plague empties Ferrara and the council is carried to Florence, where the sessions are held at Santa Maria Novella. Alberti follows the court a second time over the same road. He is standing in the church whose upper front he will be commissioned to finish some twenty years from now, when the Greeks have gone home and the union agreed here has come apart. For the moment it is a Dominican nave full of interpreters, and the wall above the door is unfinished medieval stonework that nobody has a plan for.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The Council of Florence, 1439, held at Santa Maria Novella

stops.name: Florence, the Tuscan books and the horse
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that De equo animante belongs to 1441 and that the Florentine years produced Teogenio, Della tranquillita dell'animo, Villa and the Intercenales; the individual datings within that productive period vary in the scholarship and are not fixed here. Month and day are ordering defaults. The quote is a Favole apologue in an English rendering carried on Wikiquote with no translator credited; treat the English as a working translation until traced to a named edition.
stops.campa: Settled in Florence for a stretch, he writes in Tuscan and he writes fast: Teogenio, on fortune borne without complaint; Della tranquillita dell'animo; Villa; the Intercenales, short savage fables meant for reading between courses at dinner; and a treatise on the horse, De equo animante, on breeding, training and the management of an animal a prince must be seen to command. Nothing on that list is what a chancery official is paid to produce. He produces it anyway, in the vernacular, for readers who have no Latin.
stops.quote: Envy is punished by envy itself.
stops.quote_source: Alberti, Favole, 'L'Invidioso e il Fuoco'; Italian: 'L'invidia e punita dall' invidia medesima.' English rendering as carried on Wikiquote, translator uncredited
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
en.wikiquote.org, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The Intercenales and the Tuscan moral dialogues of the Florentine years

stops.name: Florence, the Certame Coronario and no crown
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) for October 1441, the joint organization with Piero di Cosimo de' Medici, the theme of friendship, and the judges' refusal to award the crown. The day of the month is an ordering default within the attested October. The quote is not spoken here: it is the motto inscribed on Alberti's bronze self-portrait plaquette in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, generally dated about 1435, and is placed at this stop as his own device rather than as a remark made at the contest.
stops.campa: With Piero di Cosimo de' Medici he stages a public poetry contest inside Santa Maria del Fiore, open to anyone, in Tuscan, on the subject of friendship, with a silver crown for the winner. Humanists who hold that only Latin can carry a serious matter are outraged that the vernacular has been given a stage at all. The judges, secretaries of the curia, award no crown to anybody. Alberti has argued for years that Tuscan has rules and dignity of its own. The competition is not repeated.
stops.quote_source: Motto inscribed on Alberti's bronze self-portrait plaquette, National Gallery of Art, Washington; 'What then?'
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The Certame Coronario of October 1441 and the humanist quarrel over the vernacular

stops.name: Ferrara, the bronze horse and the bell tower
stops.date_confidence: The advisory relationship with the Este, covering the monument to Niccolo III (the Arco del Cavallo) and the cathedral campanile, is documented from about 1443, but the pool itself tags the division between Alberti's conception and local execution as unresolved: R, not A. The campanile attributed to him was built 1451-1493 and so belongs to 1451 and after, not to this date. Pin corrected to Ferrara Cathedral, 44.8355/11.6201 (English Wikipedia, 'Ferrara Cathedral'); the pool's 44.8369/11.6188 lay about 180 metres off toward the Castello. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: At Ferrara the Este want a monument to Niccolo III, and Alberti is consulted on the base that will carry the bronze horse in front of the cathedral. They ask him about the cathedral's bell tower as well, though no stone of that goes up before 1451. What he drew and what the local masons decided is not separable now. It is the first time a prince asks him about a building rather than a book. What survives of the transaction is a few payments and a tradition.
stops.quote: The glory of having deserved great honour is the recompense of a great soul.
stops.quote_source: Alberti, Favole, 'Il Leone e l'Invidia'; Italian: 'La gloria d'aver meritato un grand' onore e la ricompensa d'una grand' anima.' English rendering as carried on Wikiquote, translator uncredited
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Ferrara Cathedral'
suggested_refs: The Arco del Cavallo at Ferrara and the campanile of San Giorgio, 1451-1493

stops.name: Siena, the court halts on the road
stops.date_confidence: The DBI gives only 'a stop at Siena' on the return to Rome, with a June 1443 date that the pool corrects: Eugenius IV left Florence in spring 1443, lingered at Siena through the summer, and entered Rome only on 28 September. The summer dating here follows that correction; month and day are ordering defaults. Pin corrected to Siena Cathedral and the Piazza del Duomo, 43.3177/11.3290 (English Wikipedia, 'Siena Cathedral'); the pool's 43.3188/11.3306 drifted about 190 metres toward the Campo.
stops.campa: The court quits Florence in the spring and halts at Siena through the summer, waiting on the terms that will let a pope walk back into his own capital. Alberti waits with it. The record gives the stop and nothing else: no letter from Siena, no work begun there, no meeting. He has by now followed this court to Florence, to Bologna, to Ferrara, back to Florence and here. Above him the cathedral front is striped black and white, Gothic, the kind of thing he will spend the rest of his life not building.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'
English Wikipedia, 'Siena Cathedral'
suggested_refs: The return route of the curia from Florence to Rome by way of Siena, 1443

segments.name: Rome Rebuilt: Nicholas V and the Ten Books

stops.name: Rome, the entry after nine years
stops.date_confidence: Corrects the pool, which dated the return to Rome June 1443 from the DBI. Eugenius IV made his formal entry into Rome on 28 September 1443 after nearly ten years away (English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'); the DBI's June date, if it refers to anything, is the departure and the Siena leg. Alberti's return with the court is attested (DBI).
stops.campa: Eugenius IV makes his formal entry into Rome on the twenty-eighth of September, nine years and nearly four months after the boat at Ostia. The city he comes back to has lost what little order it had. Alberti returns with the chancery to the town he took down in angles before the flight, and from here the weight of his life shifts: less Tuscan moral dialogue, more antiquity, mathematics, machinery and stone. He is thirty-nine years old. Every building he is now remembered for is still ahead of him.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Pope Eugene IV'
suggested_refs: The return of the papal court to Rome, 28 September 1443

stops.name: Lake Nemi, the ships that will not rise
stops.date_confidence: The salvage attempt rests on the DBI's biographical tradition; the English Wikipedia article on Lake Nemi confirms the ships and their fame without independently detailing Alberti's attempt, and no technical drawing of his apparatus survives. Dated loosely to the middle 1440s; month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Two Roman ships lie on the floor of the crater lake at Nemi, known to be there, too deep to reach. Alberti puts together a salvage: floats, ropes, grapples, divers brought down from Genoa. They tear pieces off one hull and haul them up. The ships stay where they are. No drawing of the apparatus survives, and the operation is known from biography rather than from any account book. What came off that hull, and where it went afterwards, was never inventoried.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Lake Nemi'
suggested_refs: The Nemi ships and the fifteenth-century attempts to raise them

stops.name: Rome, an opinion on Old St Peter's
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline: Nicholas V 'commissioned work on the old building from Leone Battista Alberti and Bernardo Rossellino' (English Wikipedia, 'St. Peter's Basilica'). The source does not detail Alberti's personal contribution as against Rossellino's, and the DBI states plainly that the boundary between Alberti's advice and Rossellino's execution is often undocumentable. Nicholas V's pontificate ran 6 March 1447 to 24 March 1455; month and day are ordering defaults inside it.
stops.campa: Nicholas V, a librarian made pope, decides that the authority of the Church has to be visible in walls, and commissions work on the ancient basilica of St Peter from Bernardo Rossellino and from Alberti. The south wall of the old church is out of plumb and has been for a century. What Alberti advised, what Rossellino executed and what actually got built cannot be separated in the documents. He holds no title of architect and never will. Nicholas V dies in 1455 with the rebuilding barely out of the ground.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'St. Peter's Basilica'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Nicholas V's building programme and Bernardo Rossellino's work on Old St Peter's

stops.name: Rome, Santo Stefano Rotondo made smaller to stand
stops.date_confidence: Attested with a hedge in the source itself: 'The church was restored in the 1450s by Bernardo Rossellino, probably under the guidance of Leon Battista Alberti' (English Wikipedia, 'Santo Stefano Rotondo'). The church was entrusted to the Pauline Fathers in 1454. Month and day are ordering defaults within the decade.
stops.campa: The round church on the Caelian, built in the fifth century on a plan that had no successor, is coming down under its own weight. Rossellino restores it through the fifties, probably to Alberti's direction: the outer ring is walled off, the ancient columns are shut inside the new masonry, and the building is cut down to something that will stand. His own book will argue that the circle is the figure nature prefers above all others. The columns of the outer ring are still there, shut inside the wall.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Santo Stefano Rotondo'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: The 1450s reduction of Santo Stefano Rotondo al Celio

stops.name: Rome, the ten books presented to the pope
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI, English Wikipedia) that Alberti presented a version of De re aedificatoria to Nicholas V about 1450-1452 and went on revising it afterwards; the work stayed in manuscript through his lifetime and was first printed at Florence in 1485. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: He presents Nicholas V with the ten books on building. It is not a manual and not a copy of Vitruvius, whose text he corrects throughout: it is a treatise on how a city and its buildings should be ordered, from the choice of a site and the bearing of the winds through foundations, columns, ornament, and the public duties of a wall. Beauty in it is a matter of measure, the concinnitas from which nothing can be taken away and to which nothing can be added without harm. He keeps revising. It is not printed until 1485.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'De re aedificatoria'
suggested_refs: De re aedificatoria, presented in manuscript about 1452, first printed Florence 1485

stops.name: Rome, writing on Porcari's conspiracy
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that after Stefano Porcari's failed attempt to overthrow papal government and restore a Roman republic Alberti wrote De Porcaria coniuratione, showing sympathy for Porcari's ambition, and that no charge, investigation or punishment of Alberti is documented. Month and day are ordering defaults early in 1453. The quote is attributed to Alberti's Del Principe by Harbottle and Dalbiac (1904); Del Principe is not securely Alberti's work, and the attribution is the dictionary's, not a scholarly one. It is carried here as attributed and doubtful, not as his own words.
stops.campa: Stefano Porcari, who has argued for years that Rome should govern itself as a republic again, is taken before the rising he planned and hanged from the Castel Sant'Angelo. Alberti writes an account of the conspiracy in which the plotter's wish to restore the ancient liberty of the city is treated with respect and the method is not. Nobody charges him with anything, and no investigation of him is recorded. He keeps his place in the chancery another eleven years.
stops.quote: Nothing overshadows truth more completely than authority.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Alberti, Del Principe III, in Harbottle and Dalbiac, Dictionary of Quotations (French and Italian), 1904, p. 363; Del Principe is not securely Alberti's and the attribution is the dictionary's
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
Harbottle and Dalbiac, Dictionary of Quotations (French and Italian), 1904
suggested_refs: De Porcaria coniuratione and the Roman republican conspiracy of 1453

stops.name: Rome, the Acqua Vergine brought back to a basin
stops.date_confidence: Upgraded from the pool's R to A on the corrections: Nicholas V renovated the Aqua Virgo's main channels in 1453 and its terminus was 'a simple basin that Alberti designed, the predecessor of the Trevi Fountain', a wall fountain in the Piazza dei Crociferi (English Wikipedia, 'Acqua Vergine'; 'Pope Nicholas V'). The pin, about 60 metres from the Piazza dei Crociferi, marks the terminus site. Month and day are ordering defaults within 1453.
stops.campa: Nicholas V has the channels of the ancient Aqua Virgo cleared and running into the city again, water arriving from miles out along a conduit laid under Augustus. Restoring an aqueduct is the sort of work Alberti's own book puts first among a builder's duties, ahead of temples. At the end of the line he designs the outlet: a plain wall basin in the Piazza dei Crociferi where Romans can fill their jars. Three centuries later the Trevi is built across the same terminus and the basin is swept off it.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Acqua Vergine'
English Wikipedia, 'Pope Nicholas V'
suggested_refs: The 1453 restoration of the Aqua Virgo and Alberti's wall basin in the Piazza dei Crociferi

segments.name: Facades: Rucellai, Malatesta, and the Letter

stops.name: Florence, the front of the Palazzo Rucellai
stops.date_confidence: R, and left open. The attribution to Alberti is Vasari's and is believed by most scholars, but early sixteenth-century sources linked the design to Bernardo Rossellino instead; Schlosser, Planiscig and Charles Mack argued for Rossellino, Brenda Preyer (1981) for Alberti, and English Wikipedia calls it an open question. The pool's 'c. 1446/47-1461' is corrected to the standard 1446-1451 range (English Wikipedia, 'Palazzo Rucellai'). Coordinates verified exact. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Giovanni Rucellai, a merchant married into the Strozzi and needing a house that says so, has the front of his palace on the Via della Vigna Nuova faced in a way nothing in Florence has been faced before: three storeys of flat pilasters, one order above another, laid across the wall like the tiers of the Colosseum. Vasari gave the design to Alberti a century afterwards. Sixteenth-century sources gave it to Bernardo Rossellino. Scholars have argued both sides for a hundred years and the question is still open.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Palazzo Rucellai'
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, life of Leon Batista Alberti
suggested_refs: The disputed authorship of the Palazzo Rucellai facade: Schlosser, Planiscig, Mack against Preyer

stops.name: Rimini, the Gothic church encased in marble
stops.date_confidence: Attested (English Wikipedia, 'Tempio Malatestiano'; DBI) that Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta commissioned the reconstruction from Alberti about 1450, his first ecclesiastical work. Alberti is documented working from Rome by correspondence and is not documented on the site, so this stop marks the object he designed rather than a place he is recorded standing. Pin corrected to 44.0596/12.5702; the pool's afterlife lens carried 44.0592/12.5683, about 160 metres off. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, lord of Rimini, wants the Gothic church of San Francesco turned into something else, and Alberti gives him a shell: a marble front on the model of the Roman arch of Augustus that stands at the other end of the town, and deep arched bays down the flanks holding the sarcophagi of the court's scholars. Inside, Sigismondo's initials interlace with his mistress's and the elephants of his device carry the piers. Alberti directs the work by letter from Rome and is not documented on the site.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Tempio Malatestiano'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Matteo de' Pasti's foundation medal of 1450, the only record of the unbuilt Pantheon-scale dome

stops.name: Rome, the letter to Matteo de' Pasti
stops.date_confidence: The DBI attests a detailed 1454 letter from Alberti correcting Matteo de' Pasti's proposed departures from the Rimini design. The pool gives the year only; month and day are ordering defaults. The stop sits at Rome because that is where Alberti was writing from, not at Rimini where the letter was read. The paraphrase of its argument follows the DBI's characterization; the letter's exact wording is not quoted here because no verbatim text was reachable in this pass.
stops.campa: Matteo de' Pasti, running the work at Rimini, proposes to change the proportions of the pilasters, and Alberti answers him in writing from Rome. Alter the measures and the whole music of the thing is discomposed; the widths were taken off an antique building and the reasons for them are not arbitrary. He would rather have it left alone than improved. De' Pasti is standing at the wall with the masons; Alberti has never been documented on the site at all. The whole of the quarrel is about ratios.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Alberti's letter of 1454 to Matteo de' Pasti on the proportions of the Tempio Malatestiano

stops.name: Florence, the Holy Sepulchre in a marble box
stops.date_confidence: Attested (English Wikipedia, 'San Pancrazio, Florence'): the sepulchre was completed in 1467 by an inscription over the chapel door, and modelled after the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem's Anastasis basilica; the design range is about 1457-1467. Coordinates 43.7718/11.2500 follow the geography lens, which the corrections confirm as right against the afterlife lens's 43.7735/11.2489. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: For Giovanni Rucellai again he builds a small marble box inside the church of San Pancrazio: a chapel holding a scale model of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem, panelled all over in inlaid geometry, with a shrine inside that Rucellai means to be buried beside. The inscription over the door dates the finish to 1467. A Florentine wool merchant who never went to Jerusalem can kneel at it in his own parish, and the tomb inside is empty in exactly the way the original is.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'San Pancrazio, Florence'
suggested_refs: The Rucellai Sepulchre in the deconsecrated San Pancrazio, opened to visitors of the Museo Marino Marini from February 2013

stops.name: Florence, the tribuna of the Annunziata
stops.date_confidence: Attested (English Wikipedia, 'Santissima Annunziata, Florence'): Alberti received the commission in 1469, replacing Michelozzo, constrained by pre-existing foundations, with the Gonzaga of Mantua sponsoring the construction out of admiration for him; the work concluded in 1481, after his death. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: The Servites at the Annunziata have a half-built choir by Michelozzo and no confidence in it. Ludovico Gonzaga of Mantua, who admires Alberti, offers to pay if Alberti will design the replacement. He takes the commission working inside foundations already laid, and gives them a circular domed tribuna with chapels opening off the ring, on the model of the round temples of Rome. Florentines complain that it will darken the church. He does not live to see it closed over; the work ends in 1481, nine years after his death.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Santissima Annunziata, Florence'
suggested_refs: The Rotonda of Santissima Annunziata, begun 1469, completed 1481

stops.name: Florence, the front of Santa Maria Novella
stops.date_confidence: Attested (English Wikipedia, 'Santa Maria Novella'): commissioned by Giovanni Rucellai, begun no earlier than 1458, with a broad frieze dating the completed work to 1470 and innovative S-shaped scrolls at the corners. The right-hand scroll was clad in marble only in 1920 and the facade was restored April 2006 to March 2008; those are posthumous facts about his own work and are stated as such. Coordinates 43.7746/11.2493 are the correct ones; the afterlife lens carried 43.7764/11.2486, about 200 metres north. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Rucellai pays for the front of the Dominican church, and Alberti has to finish a facade whose lower half is thirteenth-century marble striping with tombs set into it. He does not hide it. He squares it off, puts a classical doorway in the middle, and joins the tall upper storey to the wide lower one with two great S-shaped scrolls that mask the roofs of the aisles. The frieze carries Rucellai's name and the year 1470. Architects will use those scrolls for three hundred years; the right-hand one is not faced in marble until 1920.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Santa Maria Novella'
suggested_refs: The 1470 frieze inscription of Giovanni Rucellai and the 1920 marble cladding of the right scroll

segments.name: Mantua, the Two Disks, and the Will

stops.name: Mantua, the congress that raises no crusade
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI) that Alberti travelled with the court of Pius II to the Congress of Mantua, convened to organize a crusade after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, and that he strengthened his ties to Ludovico III Gonzaga there. Pin corrected to the Palazzo Ducale, 45.16028/10.79889 rounded to 45.1603/10.7989 (English Wikipedia, 'Palazzo Ducale, Mantua'); the pool's 45.1592/10.7972 lay about 190 metres southwest. Month and day are ordering defaults within 1459.
stops.campa: Pius II summons the princes of Christendom to Mantua to organize a crusade against the Turks, six years after Constantinople fell, and gets a thin attendance and less money. Alberti comes north with the curia. Mantua is a brick town on three lakes, damp, and without one ancient monument worth measuring. Ludovico III Gonzaga, marquis of Mantua, takes to him here and will spend the rest of Alberti's life asking him for churches and paying for them. The crusade never sails.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Palazzo Ducale, Mantua'
suggested_refs: The Congress of Mantua, 1459, and the Gonzaga patronage that followed it

stops.name: Mantua, San Sebastiano on a Greek cross
stops.date_confidence: Attested (English Wikipedia, 'San Sebastiano, Mantua'; DBI): begun 1460 to Alberti's designs, a centralized Greek-cross plan with a crypt intended as a Gonzaga mausoleum, directed on site by Luca Fancelli. Construction was abandoned partway in the mid-1470s once Alberti was no longer directing it, and the present front is a reconstruction, so the original facade design is not securely known. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Gonzaga has him design a church on a Greek cross, four arms of equal length, raised over a crypt meant to hold the family's dead, with a front on no known precedent: a temple face whose entablature is broken through the middle. Luca Fancelli builds it on the ground. Nobody then or since has agreed on what that facade was meant to look like, because the work stops half done in the seventies once Alberti is no longer directing it, and what stands there now is a reconstruction.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'San Sebastiano, Mantua'
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: San Sebastiano, Mantua, begun 1460, and Luca Fancelli's site direction

stops.name: Rome, the college abolished
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI): Paul II abolished or reorganized the College of Abbreviators in 1464 and Alberti lost his chancery office. He is not documented as arrested, tried or charged, unlike some of the other dismissed humanists, and he remained in Rome, financially able to do without the salary. The priorate of San Martino a Gangalandi and the parish of Borgo San Lorenzo in the Mugello, held from 1448, are attested benefices; no document places him in residence at either. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Paul II, newly elected and hostile to the humanists crowding his chancery, abolishes the College of Abbreviators. Alberti loses the office he has held for more than thirty years. Some of the dismissed men protest, are arrested, and are later accused of conspiracy and unbelief. He is not among them, is never charged, and stays in Rome. He has benefices enough to live on, a priorate at Gangalandi and a parish in the Mugello. No record puts him in residence at either of them.
stops.quote: It is necessary to know the strong and the weak points of one's adversary, before coming to close quarters with him.
stops.quote_source: Alberti, Favole, 'Il Cane ed il Toro'; Italian: 'E necessario di conoscere il forte ed il debole del suo nemico, prima di venir con esso a cimento.' English rendering as carried on Wikiquote, translator uncredited
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
suggested_refs: Paul II's suppression of the College of Abbreviators, 1464, and the arrests of the Roman Academy

stops.name: Rome, the two disks on a pin
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI; English Wikipedia, 'Alberti cipher', 'Alberti cipher disk'): De componendis cifris was written at Leonardo Dati's prompting about 1466-67, tabulates Latin letter frequencies, and describes the Formula, a fixed outer disk (Stabilis) of capitals and four numerals with a movable inner disk (Mobilis) of a mixed lowercase alphabet. The treatise's own opening frames the device as arising from a conversation with Dati about the recently developed printing press. It is the first known European mechanical polyalphabetic cipher device, not the first cipher or cryptanalysis in world history. The al-Kindi comparison is the historiography's and not Alberti's: al-Kindi's Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma was written at Baghdad in the ninth century, and no line of Alberti's names him or shows any documented transmission. Month and day are ordering defaults. The quotation is Wikipedia's citation of A. Zaccagnini's translation, not examined in the primary edition.
stops.campa: Leonardo Dati, a papal secretary, gets him talking about the new printing press and the trade in secrets, and out of it comes a short treatise on ciphers. Alberti tabulates how often each letter falls in Latin, then defeats his own table: two copper disks on a pin, capitals and four numerals on the ring that is fixed, a scrambled lowercase alphabet on the ring that turns. Every few words the sender turns the inner disk and the substitution changes under the enemy's count. The counting of letters is not new. Al-Kindi set the method down at Baghdad six hundred years before, and nothing in Alberti names him.
stops.quote: When I have written three or four words I will change the position of the index in our formula, turning the disk until, say, the index k is under capital R.
stops.quote_source: Alberti, De componendis cifris, ch. XIV, trans. A. Zaccagnini, as quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Alberti cipher disk'
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'

English Wikipedia, 'Alberti cipher disk'

stops.name: Mantua, the design for Sant'Andrea
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI; English Wikipedia, 'Sant'Andrea, Mantua'): Ludovico Gonzaga asked Alberti for a design to replace the church housing Mantua's relic of the blood of Christ, and Alberti's surviving letter argues for his scheme in the terms quoted. Construction began in 1472, the year of his death, under Luca Fancelli. The pool's 'finished 328 years later' is corrected: construction began 1472 and completed 1790, 318 years, with Juvarra's dome added 1732-1782. Pin corrected to 45.1589/10.7942; the afterlife lens carried 45.1566/10.7914. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: Mantua keeps a relic of the blood of Christ and the pilgrims will not fit inside the old church of Sant'Andrea. Gonzaga asks for a design, and Alberti sends one with an argument attached for why it should be built his way rather than another. He proposes a single barrel-vaulted hall with chapels instead of aisles, entered through a front that is a Roman triumphal arch, and repeats the same arch down the inside walls, so that the outside and the nave are one figure stated twice. Fancelli starts building in 1472. The church is finished in 1790.
stops.quote: more capacious, more eternal, more worthy, more joyful, and less expensive
stops.quote_source: Alberti to Ludovico III Gonzaga, on his proposed design for Sant'Andrea, as reported in the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani entry
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'
English Wikipedia, 'Sant'Andrea, Mantua'

stops.name: Rome, walking the Forum with Lorenzo de' Medici
stops.date_confidence: Attested (DBI): in 1471 Alberti guided Lorenzo de' Medici, Bernardo Rucellai and Donato Acciaiuoli through the Roman Forum as an antiquarian tour. Lorenzo's presence in Rome in 1471, buying antiquities around the coronation of Sixtus IV, is independently carried on lorenzo_de_medici_il_magnifico.journey.json. Month and day are ordering defaults; nothing of what was said is recorded. The Forum pin, 41.8925/12.4853, is the same one used for the Descriptio survey.
stops.campa: Lorenzo de' Medici is in Rome for the coronation of Sixtus IV, twenty-two years old and buying antiquities, and Alberti takes him over the Forum on foot with Bernardo Rucellai and Donato Acciaiuoli. He is sixty-seven and has been reading this ground for forty years. The young man walking beside him will govern Florence for twenty more, carry away what can be carried, and pay for the scholars who read what cannot. What Alberti said among the columns that day nobody wrote down.
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Leon Battista Alberti'

stops.name: Rome, the will of the nineteenth of April
stops.date_confidence: The will is dated 19 April 1472 and by 25 April a successor had been presented to his vacant parish benefice at Borgo San Lorenzo; the DBI treats only that window as securely documented, while English Wikipedia states 25 April as the death date and other modern sources give 20 April. The disagreement is recorded and not resolved. The testamentary wish for burial at Sant'Agostino and transfer to his father's tomb at Padua is attested in the will (Italian Wikipedia, 'Leon Battista Alberti'); its execution is not.
stops.campa: He makes his will on the nineteenth of April. In it he asks to be buried at Sant'Agostino in Rome and then carried to Padua, to lie beside his father, dead fifty-one years and lying there since. Six days later the parish of Borgo San Lorenzo in the Mugello is presented with a new priest, which is how the date of his death is known: not from any record of the death, but from the filling of the office it emptied. Modern books give 20 April and 25 April with equal confidence. He is sixty-eight.
stops.quote: Leon Batista Alberti was a man of refined habits and praiseworthy life, a friend of distinguished men, liberal and courteous to all.
stops.quote_source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, life of Leon Batista Alberti, trans. Mrs Jonathan Foster (Bohn)

stops.name: Rome, Sant'Agostino and no trace of the grave
stops.date_confidence: R, and the pool's own correction insists on it: Italian Wikipedia states that by his testament Alberti wished to be buried at Sant'Agostino and then transferred to his father's tomb at Padua, 'ma non sono rimaste tracce della sepoltura', no traces of the burial remain. The interment is therefore a documented wish of unverified execution, not a documented fact, and the pool's afterlife lens overstated it. Pin corrected to the Basilica of Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio, 41.90083/12.47417 rounded to 41.9008/12.4742. The church was rebuilt 1479-1483. The 1485 printing is attested (English Wikipedia, 'De re aedificatoria').
stops.campa: The church of Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio takes the body, if the will was carried out. Seven years later the church is pulled down and rebuilt, and no monument, no slab and no notice of any transfer to Padua survives; the Italian record says plainly that no trace of the burial remains. There is no grave anyone can point to. In 1485 the ten books are printed at Florence, the first architectural treatise ever set in type, a year ahead of Vitruvius.
